questions.question: In a STARK-style system, what is the trace table?
options: A table of per-step register values that claims to be the computation’s execution
A table of elliptic-curve points that encodes the proving key
A table of random challenges sampled by the verifier before seeing any commitment
A table of hashes that replaces the need for any algebraic constraints
questions.explanation: A trace is the prover’s claimed execution: rows are steps, columns are registers, all over a field.

questions.question: What does a Merkle commitment (Merkle root) primarily give you in a proof system?
options: A binding commitment to many values with short inclusion proofs for a few opened values
A way to make polynomial evaluation faster than O(n)
A guarantee that the committed data forms a low-degree polynomial codeword
A trusted setup ceremony that generates toxic waste
questions.explanation: A Merkle root binds the prover to the full dataset and supports logarithmic-size openings for sampled positions.

questions.question: Which constraint type pins specific rows (like row 0) to expected values?
options: Boundary constraints
Transition constraints
Permutation constraints
Lookup constraints
questions.explanation: Boundary constraints enforce conditions at designated rows, typically the first and/or last rows.

questions.question: In the Fibonacci AIR with registers (x0, x1), which transition rule is enforced from row i to row i+1?
options: y0 = x1 and y1 = x0 + x1 (mod p)
y0 = x0 + x1 and y1 = x1 (mod p)
y0 = x0 and y1 = x1 (mod p)
y0 = x0 * x1 and y1 = x0 + x1 (mod p)
questions.explanation: The next state shifts x1 into x0 and updates x1 to the sum of the previous two values.

questions.question: What is the role of Fiat–Shamir in the toy protocol in this lesson?
options: Derive deterministic query positions from the commitment so the proof can be non-interactive
Encrypt the trace so the verifier cannot see any opened values
Replace Merkle trees with polynomial commitments automatically
Guarantee post-quantum security even if the hash function is weak
questions.explanation: Fiat–Shamir turns verifier randomness into hashes of the transcript/commitment, binding challenges to what was committed.

questions.question: What major component is missing from the toy protocol that a full STARK uses to enforce polynomial structure?
options: A low-degree test such as FRI
An elliptic-curve pairing check
A trusted setup ceremony
A group signature scheme
questions.explanation: Full STARKs use a low-degree test (commonly FRI) so the committed evaluations must come from a low-degree polynomial.

questions.question: Why are spot checks alone not enough to make this toy protocol a full STARK?
options: A prover can craft an arbitrary table that passes a few local checks but is not a low-degree encoding of any trace polynomial
A Merkle tree cannot commit to more than 2^16 leaves
Fiat–Shamir only works with elliptic-curve commitments
Boundary constraints are impossible to check without revealing the entire trace
questions.explanation: Without low-degree enforcement, the prover can commit to a table that is locally consistent at sampled points but globally invalid as a polynomial codeword.

questions.question: Attack mindset: if the verifier forgets to check the boundary condition (row 0), what is a realistic failure mode?
options: The prover can start from a different initial state and still satisfy many transition checks
The prover can invert SHA-256 and forge arbitrary Merkle roots
The verifier becomes unable to compute any Fiat–Shamir challenges
The trace becomes automatically low-degree even without FRI
questions.explanation: If the initial state is unconstrained, many incorrect executions can satisfy the same transition rule while proving the wrong statement.
